title: Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis (SD3)

pages.title: A straight line from noise to image
pages.subtitle: What SD3 changes and why it matters

blocks.html: The problem. Diffusion models (DDPM, Stable Diffusion, the earlier papers in this collection) generate an image by reversing a noising process: start from pure Gaussian noise and take many tiny denoising steps. The standard formulation defines a curved, stochastic path between data and noise, and the way you space the timesteps and weight the loss during training is mostly inherited convention. This paper asks two practical questions: (1) can we use a simpler, straighter path from noise to data, and (2) can we redesign the network so that text and image truly talk to each other, then scale the whole thing up cleanly?

The intuition / analogy. Imagine you want to travel from a city (pure noise) to a destination (a clean image). A classical diffusion path is a winding mountain road — to follow it accurately you need many small careful steps. Rectified Flow instead lays down a straight highway: the model is trained so the trajectory between noise and data is as close to a straight line as possible. A straight line is the easiest curve to follow with few steps, so sampling gets faster and more robust. The paper's job is to make that highway actually train well at scale.

items: Rectified Flow (RF): connect data and noise with a straight-line interpolation and train the network to predict the constant velocity along it.
Better timestep sampling: RF's hard work is concentrated in the middle of the trajectory, so they bias training toward middle timesteps with new noise schedulers (logit-normal, mode, CosMap).
MM-DiT: a new Multimodal Diffusion Transformer that gives text tokens and image tokens their own weights but lets them attend to each other — a two-way street, not text-conditioning bolted on.
Scaling: they scale to 8B parameters and show validation loss predicts sample quality, with no sign of saturation.

blocks.html: Rectified flow is a recent generative model formulation that connects data and noise in a straight line. Despite its better theoretical properties and conceptual simplicity, it is not yet decisively established as standard practice. In this work, we improve existing noise sampling techniques for training rectified flow models by biasing them towards perceptually relevant scales.

Why it mattered. This is the architecture and training recipe behind Stable Diffusion 3. It took rectified flow — a clean idea that had not yet beaten classical diffusion in practice — and, with the right timestep weighting and a genuinely multimodal transformer, made it state-of-the-art for text-to-image at the time, surpassing DALL·E 3, Midjourney v6, and Ideogram v1 on typography and prompt following in human evaluation.

pages.title: Flows, ODEs, and the conditional flow-matching trick
pages.subtitle: How a velocity field replaces the noise predictor

blocks.html: The question this page answers. DDPM-style models think in terms of a stochastic chain of noisy images. Flow models think in terms of a smooth trajectory governed by an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Before we can talk about straightening that trajectory, we need to define it. What exactly is the network learning, and how do you train it without ever solving the expensive integral?

The setup. Generative modeling defines a path $p_t$ that morphs the simple noise distribution $p_1 = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ at time $t=1$ into the data distribution $p_0$ at time $t=0$. This path is generated by an ODE driven by a velocity field $v$:

Here $z_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the sample at time $t \in [0,1]$ (a latent of the same shape as the image latent), $v_\Theta(z_t, t)$ is the velocity predicted by a neural network with parameters $\Theta$, and $dt$ is an infinitesimal time step. Reading it plainly: at every point and time, the network tells you which direction and how fast to move. Generate by starting at noise $z_1$ and integrating this ODE backward to $z_0$.

The trick — define the path per-sample, not globally. Directly regressing $v_\Theta$ onto the true marginal velocity is intractable. Flow Matching fixes this by defining a conditional path for each individual data point $x_0$, which gives a closed-form target. The paper writes the per-sample interpolation as $z_t = a_t x_0 + b_t \epsilon$, where $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ is a fresh noise sample, and $a_t, b_t$ are scalar schedules (with $a_0=1, b_0=0$ so $z_0=x_0$, and $a_1=0, b_1=1$ so $z_1=\epsilon$). The Conditional Flow Matching loss is:

Term by term: $v_\Theta(z,t)$ is the network's predicted velocity (shape $\mathbb{R}^d$); $u_t(z\,|\,\epsilon)$ is the conditional target velocity — the exact time-derivative of the chosen interpolation, a known formula, not something you have to estimate; the expectation $\mathbb{E}$ averages over time $t$, over noise $\epsilon$, and over the resulting noisy point $z$. The key theorem (Lipman et al., 2023) is that this tractable conditional loss has the same gradient as the intractable marginal one — so minimizing it learns the correct global velocity field.

Why it works. The conditional target $u_t$ is computable in closed form because, conditioned on a specific $x_0$ and $\epsilon$, the trajectory is fully determined. You never solve an ODE during training: you sample a $t$, build $z_t$ by interpolation, and regress the network's velocity onto the analytic target. This is the same spirit as DDPM's 'just predict the noise' simplification, but phrased in continuous-time velocity terms, which is what lets us reason about the shape of the path.

Context. Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2022), Rectified Flow (Liu et al., 2022), and Stochastic Interpolants (Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2022) arrived almost simultaneously in 2022 as a unifying, continuous-normalizing-flow view of diffusion. SD3's contribution is not inventing these — it is the careful empirical study of which path and which timestep weighting actually wins at billion-parameter scale.

pages.title: Rectified Flow: the straight-line path
pages.subtitle: One formulation to rule them all

blocks.html: The question. The previous page left the schedules $a_t, b_t$ open — there are many valid choices (DDPM's variance-preserving path, EDM, the cosine schedule, and others). Each defines a differently-shaped curve from noise to data. Which one is best? SD3 argues for the simplest possible answer: a straight line.

Concrete example. Suppose your data point is the number $x_0 = 4$ and your noise draw is $\epsilon = 10$. Rectified Flow says the trajectory is just the straight interpolation $z_t = (1-t)\cdot 4 + t\cdot 10$. At $t=0$ you are at $4$ (the data), at $t=1$ you are at $10$ (the noise), and at $t=0.5$ you are exactly halfway at $7$. The velocity is the constant $10 - 4 = 6$ everywhere — no curvature, no acceleration. That constant is precisely the target the network must learn to predict.

Reading it: $z_t$ is the point on the line at fraction $t$; $(1-t)$ is the weight on the clean data $x_0$; $t$ is the weight on the noise $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$. As $t$ runs $0 \to 1$ you slide linearly from data to noise. Comparing to the general form $z_t = a_t x_0 + b_t \epsilon$, Rectified Flow simply picks $a_t = 1-t$ and $b_t = t$ — the two straightest schedules possible.

The target velocity is a constant. Differentiating the line with respect to $t$ gives $u_t = \frac{d z_t}{dt} = \epsilon - x_0$, which does not depend on $t$ at all. So the RF objective corresponds to a specific loss weighting; the paper notes the RF loss matches $\mathcal{L}_{CFM}$ with a weighting $w_t^{RF} = \frac{t}{1-t}$, which connects it to other formulations through a single shared lens.

Here $u_t$ is the conditional target velocity the network regresses onto; $\epsilon$ is the noise endpoint and $x_0$ the data endpoint. Because it is constant along the whole path, the network is being asked to learn the simplest possible signal — the displacement vector from data to noise — rather than a velocity that changes shape over time.

Why a straight line wins. An ODE solver approximates the true trajectory with discrete steps; the error of each step grows with the curvature of the path. A straight line has zero curvature, so in principle a single large step is exact. Curved diffusion paths (EDM, cosine, VP) force you to take many small steps to control error. By straightening the path, RF makes few-step sampling far more accurate — fewer network evaluations for the same quality. The trade-off, addressed next, is that with real (non-conditional) data the learned field is not perfectly straight, so the where of training effort still matters.

Context & trivia. 'Rectified' literally means 'made straight.' Liu et al. (2022) showed you can even iterate the procedure (reflow) to straighten further. SD3 deliberately does not rely on reflow; it shows that a single well-trained rectified flow, with the right timestep sampling, already beats the curved alternatives — making it the practical default rather than a theoretical curiosity.

pages.title: Where to spend training effort: timestep samplers
pages.subtitle: Logit-normal, mode, and CosMap weighting

blocks.html: The question. If the path is straight, what is left to tune? The answer is which timesteps you train on. In a uniform schedule you'd sample $t$ evenly across $[0,1]$, treating the moment-of-pure-noise and the moment-of-nearly-clean-image as equally important. SD3 argues they are not — and reweighting where the model practices is one of its biggest empirical wins.

The intuition. At $t=0$ the input is the clean image, at $t=1$ it is pure noise. At both ends the prediction is easy: near $t=0$ the velocity is almost trivially recoverable, and near $t=1$ the optimal answer is essentially the dataset mean. The genuinely hard, information-rich decisions — overall layout, object shapes, coarse structure — happen in the middle of the trajectory. The paper states this directly:

Intuitively, the resulting velocity prediction target $\epsilon - x_0$ is more difficult for $t$ in the middle of $[0,1]$, since for $t=0$ the optimal prediction is the mean of $p_1$, and for $t=1$ the optimal prediction is the mean of $p_0$.

The fix — sample $t$ from a peaked distribution. Instead of uniform $t$, draw it from a density $\pi(t)$ that concentrates on the middle. The training loss for RF then becomes a reweighted objective $\mathcal{L}_{w_t^{RF}}$, where giving more weight to intermediate timesteps is equivalent to sampling them more frequently:

Term by term: $w_t^\pi$ is the effective loss weight at timestep $t$; $\frac{t}{1-t}$ is the intrinsic RF weighting from the straight-line path; and $\pi(t)$ is the timestep sampling density you get to choose. The insight is that changing how often you sample a timestep is the same as changing its loss weight — so you control emphasis simply by choosing $\pi(t)$.

Concrete choice — logit-normal. SD3's best-performing default is the logit-normal sampler: draw a normal variable, push it through a sigmoid so it lands in $(0,1)$, and use that as $t$. Its mean $m$ shifts the peak and its width $s$ controls how sharply training concentrates near the middle. They also test a mode sampler (a heavy-tailed density with a tunable peak that can still touch the endpoints) and the CosMap sampler, which reparameterizes the cosine schedule into RF coordinates via

where $u$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ and $f$ maps it to a timestep $t$ whose induced density matches the cosine schedule's log-SNR spacing. The point of listing three is that SD3 ran a controlled bake-off across all of them.

Why it works / what breaks without it. With uniform $t$, the model wastes capacity on the easy endpoints and under-trains the hard middle, hurting both sample quality and few-step robustness. Biasing toward the middle directly targets the perceptually important scales. In the sweep, rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00) — logit-normal centered at the middle — ranks at or near the top across step budgets, and plain uniform rf ranks far down the table. This single design choice is what turns rectified flow from 'theoretically nice' into 'practically best.'

pages.title: MM-DiT: a two-way street between text and image
pages.subtitle: Separate weights, joint attention

blocks.html: The question this page answers. A text-to-image model has to fuse two very different streams: a sequence of text tokens (from a language encoder) and a grid of image latent tokens. Earlier diffusion models inject text by cross-attention — image tokens look at text, but text never looks back, and the same network weights process both. SD3 argues both modalities deserve first-class treatment, because they have genuinely different statistics and need different processing.

The analogy. Think of a translator and a painter working together. With old-style cross-attention, the painter occasionally glances at the translator's notes but the translator never sees the canvas — communication is one-way. MM-DiT seats them at the same table: the painter (image stream) and the translator (text stream) each keep their own tools (separate weights), but they share one conversation (a joint attention operation) so each can react to the other in real time.

The three text encoders. The caption is encoded by three models in parallel: CLIP-L/14, CLIP-G/14, and the large T5-XXL. The two CLIP models supply a pooled global vector; their token sequences (77 + 77 tokens) plus T5's tokens are concatenated along the channel dimension into a 4096-channel context representation $c$. The pooled CLIP vector and the diffusion timestep are combined into a global conditioning vector $y$ that modulates every block.

items: Image stream: the noised latent is split into patches, linearly embedded, and given positional embeddings — producing image tokens $x$ (the painter's canvas).
Text stream: the concatenated CLIP+T5 token sequence is linearly projected to the model width — producing context tokens $c$ (the translator's notes).
Two sets of weights: each MM-DiT block has independent normalization, projection, and MLP weights for the text tokens versus the image tokens — they are not forced to share parameters.

One joint attention: the queries, keys, and values from both streams are concatenated and attended together in a single self-attention, so text attends to image and image attends to text symmetrically.

blocks.html: Modulation by timestep and pooled text. Following DiT, each block is conditioned on the global vector $y$ (timestep embedding + pooled CLIP) through adaptive layer-norm: $y$ is mapped to per-block scale and shift parameters that modulate the activations. This is how the model knows how noisy the current input is and what the overall caption gist is, separate from the fine-grained token-level context $c$.

Since text and image embeddings are conceptually quite different, we use two separate sets of weights for the two modalities. As shown in Figure 2b, this is equivalent to having two independent transformers for each modality, but joining the sequences for the attention operation, such that both representations can work in their own space yet take the other one into account.

Why it works / what breaks without it. Sharing weights between modalities forces the network to compromise between two different statistical regimes; one-way cross-attention starves the text representation of visual feedback. MM-DiT's separate-weights-but-joint-attention design lets each stream specialize while still exchanging information every layer. In their scaling study this architecture both trained more stably and reached lower validation loss than DiT, UViT, and cross-attention baselines.

Context. MM-DiT is a descendant of the Diffusion Transformer (DiT, Peebles & Xie, 2023), which replaced the U-Net backbone with a pure transformer and showed compute scales smoothly. SD3's twist — bidirectional joint attention across modalities — was influential beyond images: the 'give each modality its own weights but share attention' pattern reappears in later multimodal generative systems. The image tokens, crucially, use 2D positional embeddings, and the model uses a latent with more channels than SD1/SD2 (see next page) to preserve fine detail.

pages.title: Better inputs: a wider autoencoder and synthetic captions
pages.subtitle: Two quiet upgrades that move the needle

blocks.html: The question. Architecture aside, the diffusion model only ever sees two things: the latent the autoencoder hands it, and the caption the text encoder hands it. SD3 improves both — and these turn out to matter as much as the flow formulation.

Upgrade 1 — a higher-capacity latent space. Like Stable Diffusion, SD3 operates in the latent space of a VAE that downsamples the image by a factor of 8. Earlier SD used a 4-channel latent. SD3 widens this to 16 channels. Intuition: each latent 'pixel' must summarize an 8x8 image patch, and 4 numbers is a tight budget for that — fine textures and small text get crushed. More channels means a richer summary and a more faithful reconstruction before the diffusion model even starts.

Reading the table (reconstruction quality of the autoencoder, downsampling factor 8): going from 4 to 16 channels cuts reconstruction FID from 2.41 to 1.06 and roughly halves perceptual error, while SSIM and PSNR rise. The cost is a slightly harder distribution for the diffusion model to learn — but the paper shows the larger models comfortably absorb the extra channels, so the net effect is sharper detail and far better small-text rendering.

Upgrade 2 — synthetic captions. Web alt-text is short and noisy ('IMG_2024.jpg', or a few keywords). SD3 re-captions images with a vision-language model (CogVLM) to get rich, descriptive sentences, then trains on a 50/50 mix of original and synthetic captions. The mix matters: training purely on synthetic captions makes the model forget rare visual concepts that only appear in the original web corpus.

Reading the table: with a 50/50 caption mix, overall GenEval success rises from 43.3% to 49.8%, with the biggest jumps on the compositional skills that need detailed descriptions — color attribution (11.8% to 24.8%) and spatial position (6.5% to 18.0%). These are exactly the prompts where short alt-text gives the model nothing to learn from.

Why it works. Both upgrades follow the same logic: give the model a cleaner, higher-information signal. A wider latent preserves detail the model would otherwise have no way to recover; dense captions teach attributes and spatial relations that web text omits. The 50/50 ratio is the calibration knob — enough synthetic data to teach detail, enough original data to retain coverage of the long tail.

Context. The synthetic-caption trick echoes DALL·E 3's caption-improvement paper (2023), which argued that prompt-following is bottlenecked by caption quality, not model capacity. SD3 confirms it quantitatively on GenEval and adopts it as standard practice.

pages.title: Scaling laws and a bake-off of formulations
pages.subtitle: Loss predicts quality; rectified flow wins

blocks.html: The question. Two empirical claims have to hold for the recipe to be worth it: (1) among all the path/weighting formulations, the rectified-flow + logit-normal choice should actually be best, and (2) scaling the model up should keep paying off predictably. SD3 tests both with large controlled sweeps.

The bake-off. They train 61 different formulations — epsilon/v-prediction with linear or cosine schedules, EDM, and rectified flow with various timestep samplers — on ImageNet and CC12M, then rank each by averaged CLIP and FID across sampling-step budgets. The clean winners are the rectified-flow variants with concentrated, middle-biased timestep sampling.

Reading the table (lower rank = better, averaged over ImageNet + CC12M, EMA and non-EMA): the logit-normal rectified flow centered on the middle of the trajectory ranks #1 overall and is especially dominant in the aggressive 5-step regime (rank 1.25), where straight paths pay off most. Plain uniform-$t$ rectified flow sits in the middle of the pack, and the classic v/linear diffusion baseline is near the bottom — concrete evidence that the timestep weighting, not just the straight path, is doing the work.

The scaling study. They train a ladder of MM-DiT models up to 8 billion parameters (depth $d$ from 15 up to 38 blocks) and find a smooth relationship between training compute, validation loss, and human-judged quality.

We observe a smooth decrease in the validation loss with increasing model size and training steps... Importantly, we find that the validation loss is a strong predictor of overall model performance and that this correlation holds across the broad range of model sizes we consider.

Why this matters. The validation-loss-predicts-quality result is the load-bearing claim for any scaling effort: it means you can pick architectures and recipes by a cheap loss number instead of running expensive human evaluations each time, and you can extrapolate. Critically, the curves do not saturate in the range tested — bigger models and more compute were still improving, which is exactly the green light needed to justify training a flagship model.

Trade-off / trivia. Larger models also need fewer sampling steps to reach a given quality, so the scaling win compounds: the 8B model is both better and more sample-efficient. This mirrors the language-model scaling laws (Chinchilla, in this collection) that SD3 explicitly draws on — the same 'loss is a clean, predictable function of scale' philosophy, now demonstrated for rectified-flow image transformers.

pages.title: State of the art and lasting impact
pages.subtitle: Beating DALL·E 3 and Midjourney on prompts and text

blocks.html: The payoff. All the pieces — straight-line rectified flow, middle-biased logit-normal timesteps, the MM-DiT two-way architecture, the 16-channel latent, and the 50/50 synthetic captions — combine into the 8B flagship. In human preference evaluation it set a new bar for open text-to-image models.

What humans preferred. Evaluators compared SD3 against the leading systems on three axes: visual aesthetics, prompt following, and typography (rendering legible text in the image). SD3 came out ahead of DALL·E 3, Midjourney v6, and Ideogram v1.
Based on human preference evaluation, we compare the largest model with various open and closed-source models and find that it outperforms current state-of-the-art text-to-image generation systems.

items: Prompt following: MM-DiT's bidirectional text-image attention plus T5-XXL conditioning yields strong compositional accuracy — counting, spatial position, and attribute binding (validated on GenEval).
Typography: the wider latent and dense captions let SD3 render readable words and signs, historically a glaring failure mode of diffusion models.
Few-step sampling: the straightened trajectory means high quality with far fewer ODE steps than curved-path diffusion.
Flexible resolutions: the patch-based transformer plus 2D positional embeddings handle varying aspect ratios cleanly.

blocks.html: Why it mattered / influence. SD3 was the open release that made rectified flow the mainstream choice for high-resolution generation. The MM-DiT backbone and the flow-matching-with-logit-normal-timesteps recipe became the template for the generation that followed — including Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX, and the broader shift across the field from curved diffusion schedules to flow matching. It is the bridge between the DiT idea (transformers for diffusion) and the modern multimodal generative stack.

Trivia. The paper's title is a triple pun on 'rectified' (straightened paths), 'flow' (the flow-matching objective), and 'scaling' (the headline 8B scaling study). And despite all the theory, the single most impactful empirical knob was almost embarrassingly simple: which timesteps you train on — sample the middle of the noise-to-data path more often, and everything downstream improves.
